### Performance

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Binary size | 34 MB (release, stripped, LTO) |
| RAM idle (RSS) | 57 MB |
| RAM active (100 msgs) | ~20 MB |
| Startup time | < 50 ms |
| Database ops | < 10 ms (session), < 5 ms (message) |
| Embedding engine | embeddinggemma-300M (~300 MB, local GGUF, auto-downloaded) or any OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings`API |

#### Memory Search (qmd — FTS5 + Vector Embeddings)

Hybrid semantic search: FTS5 BM25 keyword matching + vector embeddings combined via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Three modes: local GGUF (default, no API key), OpenAI-compatible API, or FTS5-only (VPS-friendly).

Benchmarked with `cargo bench --bench memory` on release builds:

| Operation | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Store open | 1.81 ms | Cold start (create DB + schema) |
| Index file | 214 µs | Insert content + document |
| Hash skip | 19.5 µs | Already indexed, unchanged — fast path |
| FTS search (10 docs) | 397 µs | 2-term BM25 query |
| FTS search (50 docs) | 2.57 ms | Typical user corpus |
| FTS search (100 docs) | 9.22 ms | |
| FTS search (500 docs) | 88.1 ms | Large corpus |
| Vector search (10 docs) | 247 µs | 768-dim cosine similarity |
| Vector search (50 docs) | 1.02 ms | 768-dim cosine similarity |
| Vector search (100 docs) | 2.04 ms | 768-dim cosine similarity |
| Hybrid RRF (50 docs) | 3.49 ms | FTS + vector → Reciprocal Rank Fusion |
| Insert embedding | 301 µs | Single 768-dim vector |
| Bulk reindex (50 files) | 11.4 ms | From cold, includes store open |
| Deactivate document | 267 µs | Prune a single entry |

**Benchmarks** (release build, in-memory SQLite, criterion):

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| Index 50 files (first run) | 11.4 ms |
| Per-file index | 214 µs |
| Hash skip (unchanged file) | 19.5 µs |
| FTS search (10 docs) | 397 µs |
| FTS search (50 docs) | 2.57 ms |
| FTS search (100 docs) | 9.2 ms |
| Vector search (10 docs, 768-dim) | 247 µs |
| Vector search (50 docs, 768-dim) | 1.02 ms |
| Vector search (100 docs, 768-dim) | 2.04 ms |
| Hybrid RRF (FTS + vector, 50 docs) | 3.49 ms |
| Insert embedding | 301 µs |
| Deactivate document | 267 µs |

## 🐛 Platform Notes

Automated setup:Run`src/scripts/setup.sh`to detect your platform and install everything automatically.

### Linux

```
# Debian/Ubuntu
# Fedora/RHEL
# Arch
```
#### Older CPUs (Sandy Bridge / AVX-only)

The default release binary requires AVX2 (Haswell 2013+). If you have an older CPU with only AVX support (Sandy Bridge/Ivy Bridge, 2011-2012), build from source with:

```
RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native"
```
Pre-built `*-compat` binaries are also available on the [releases page](https://github.com/adolfousier/opencrabs/releases) for AVX-only CPUs. If your CPU lacks AVX entirely (pre-2011), or you're on a low-RAM VPS, set `vector_enabled = false` in `[memory]` to disable vector embeddings and use FTS5-only keyword search.

### macOS

Requires **macOS 15 (Sequoia)** or later.

```
# Install build dependencies
```
#### Metal GPU crash on macOS 14 (Sonoma) or older

If you see this error when running OpenCrabs:

```
dyld: Symbol not found: _OBJC_CLASS_$_MTLResidencySetDescriptor
```
This happens because `llama.cpp` (used for local embeddings) compiles with Metal GPU support and unconditionally links Metal frameworks that require macOS 15+. There is currently no way to disable Metal at build time through the Rust `llama-cpp-sys-2` crate.

**Fix:** Update to macOS 15 (Sequoia) or later.

### Windows

Requires CMake, NASM, and Visual Studio Build Tools for native crypto dependencies:

```
# Option 1: Install build tools
# - CMake (add to PATH)
# - NASM (add to PATH)
# - Visual Studio Build Tools ("Desktop development with C++")
# Option 2: Use WSL2 (recommended)
```
See [BUILD_NOTES.md](https://docs.rs/src/docs/guides/BUILD_NOTES.md) for detailed troubleshooting.

## 🔧 Troubleshooting

### Telegram Won't Connect / Reconnect

If the Telegram bot stops responding or you need to re-link it, re-run the channels setup and re-confirm the token + your numeric user ID.

**Fix:**

- Run `/onboard:channels`(TUI: opens the wizard; on a channel: the agent walks you through it).
- Paste your **bot token**again if it's missing (get it from[@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather)).
- Paste your **numeric user ID**and hit Enter to confirm.
- If the bot sends you a message on Telegram, it worked.

On a channel you can do it in one line: `/onboard:channels telegram <BOT_TOKEN> <YOUR_NUMERIC_ID>`.

**Why you have to provide your numeric ID:** Telegram's Bot API exposes only the *bot's* identity from a token (via `getMe`) — it has **no way to reveal who created the bot** in BotFather. A bot only learns a human's ID when that human messages it (the incoming update carries the sender's ID). The onboarding wizard auto-detects your ID via `getUpdates` when you leave the field blank, **but** that only works if (a) you've already messaged the bot and (b) the bot isn't already running and consuming those updates — which is exactly the case during a *reconnect*. So on reconnect, message the bot first, or just paste the ID (get it from [@userinfobot](https://t.me/userinfobot)).

### WhatsApp Won't Connect / Wrong Number Replying

Each OpenCrabs instance supports **one WhatsApp account** (one companion device). If you connected multiple numbers or the wrong number is replying, you need to do a full reset before connecting a new number. The bot always uses the **last number you connected**, so if you tried multiple, only the most recent one replies.

**The bot talks to itself:** Like Telegram DMs, if you message the bot's own paired number, the bot replies to you. This is by design. The paired account's self-chat is always allowed.

**Allowlist behavior:** Anyone messaging the paired number who is on the `allowed_phones` list gets a reply. The `response_policy` (`auto`/`owner_only`/`allowlist`/`open`) controls who else can interact.

Critical:Always reset the connection before connecting a new number. OpenCrabs only keeps the last paired number.

**Full reset steps (required before connecting a new number):**

- **Remove the OpenCrabs device from WhatsApp**— open WhatsApp on your phone, go to- **Settings → Linked Devices**, find the- `opencrabs`device, and- **remove it**. This is mandatory.
- **Reset the connection in OpenCrabs**— in the TUI or from a channel, go to- `/onboard:channels`and press- **R**to reset the WhatsApp connection. Wait for confirmation that the reset is complete.
- **Re-pair from scratch**— after the reset is confirmed, go to WhatsApp →- **Settings → Linked Devices**→- **Link a Device**and scan the new QR code shown by OpenCrabs.

If the bot still shows the old number after resetting, make sure you completed step 1 (removing the device from WhatsApp) before step 2.

**Common issues:**

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Old number still replying | Old device not removed from WhatsApp app | Remove `opencrabs`from WhatsApp → Settings → Linked Devices, then pressRin`/onboard:channels` |
| QR code doesn't appear | Agent is still connected (no restart triggered) | Press Rin`/onboard:channels`to force a restart, then wait for the new QR |
| Bot doesn't reply to anyone | `response_policy`is too restrictive | Set `response_policy = "allowlist"`and add phone numbers to`allowed_phones`in`config.toml` |
| Bot replies to everyone | `response_policy`is`open` | Set `response_policy = "allowlist"`or`"owner_only"`in`config.toml` |
| Bot doesn't reply to self-chat | `allowed_phones`doesn't include the paired number | The paired number's self-chat is always allowed, regardless of `allowed_phones`. If it's not working, check that`response_policy`isn't`dm_only`with no owner set |

### Agent Hallucinating Tool Calls

If the agent starts sending tool call approvals that don't render in the UI — meaning it believes it executed actions that never actually ran — the session context has become corrupted.

**Fix:** Start a new session.

- Press `/`and type`sessions`(or navigate to the Sessions panel)
- Press **N**to create a new session
- Continue your work in the fresh session

This reliably resolves the issue. A fix is coming in a future release.

### Windows Defender Blocking OpenCrabs

Windows Defender (or other antivirus software) may flag `opencrabs.exe` as suspicious because it's an unsigned binary that executes shell commands and makes network requests. This is a false positive.

**Fix — Add an exclusion:**

- Open **Windows Security**→**Virus & threat protection**
- Scroll to **Virus & threat protection settings**→**Manage settings**
- Scroll to **Exclusions**→**Add or remove exclusions**
- Click **Add an exclusion**→**File**→ select`opencrabs.exe`

**Or via PowerShell (admin):**

```
Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\path\to\opencrabs.exe"
```
If SmartScreen blocks the first run, click **More info** → **Run anyway**.

# dent8_store - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dent8-store/0.1.0/dent8_store/

A projection of every claim stream for one entity, folded independently and keyed
by claim_id. Built by replay_entity (or replay_entity_with_policy) from
the entity’s events in global order. Unlike per-claim replay, this view enables
cross-stream checks such as EntityProjection::lineage_issues.

A still-believed claim that transitively derives (EvidenceKind::DerivedFrom, ADR 0010)
from a claim now in a terminal invalidated lifecycle (Retracted/Expired) — i.e. poison
(or a removed source) that survived in a derivative. root is an invalidated source the
taint traces to.

The structural difference between a baseline projection and a counterfactual one,
computed by diff_states. Powers “what changes if I distrust source X / raise
the authority or confidence floor” queries over the same log.

The async counterpart to EventStore, for backends that do network or embedded-DB
I/O (Postgres, SQLite via sqlx, …). It carries the same firewall contract: every
implementation MUST arbitrate each candidate (arbitrate_events) inside its
transaction before persisting — there is no un-arbitrated write path.

Compare a baseline projection against a counterfactual one (both folded from the
same log, under different policies). The arguments read base-then-counterfactual.

Fold an ordered claim-event stream into its current projected state. Strict: a
stream that does not start with claim.asserted surfaces the transition error.

Re-fold a claim-event stream under an EpistemicPolicy. Non-admitted events are
skipped as if they never occurred; if the asserting event is filtered out the
claim is absent (Ok(None)) under this policy.

Entity-level replay_entity under an EpistemicPolicy: each stream is folded
under the policy, so a distrusted source can make whole claims absent from the
entity view — the multi-claim counterfactual surface.

Cross-entity retraction-taint analysis over the whole log: fold every claim stream to
its lifecycle and collect its DerivedFrom dependency edges, then report each
still-believed claim that transitively depends on an invalidated (Retracted/Expired)
source. This is the read-side “poison does not survive in derivatives” check (ADR 0010) —
computed on replay, never written, and cross-entity (a dependency may live in another
subject’s stream).

# dent8_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dent8-core/0.1.0/dent8_core/

## Expand description

Core domain model for dent8.

The public model intentionally starts with claim events rather than memory items. Materialized memory is a replayed projection of the event log.

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.7

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.7/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

# openipc_video - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openipc-video/0.1.28/openipc_video/

## Expand description

Low-latency platform video decoding for OpenIPC applications.

The crate accepts complete Annex-B access units, keeps codec parsing and backpressure behavior platform-neutral, and delegates actual decoding to a platform decoder. H.264 and H.265 are supported by the shared API.

- Platform decoder implementations and their retained surface types. Target decoder backends for desktop, Android, and WebAssembly.

- Small queue, mailbox, and RTP timestamp utilities for decode runtimes. Reusable bounded buffering and timestamp helpers for decoder integrations.

# retry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/retry/2.2.0/target-redirect/retry/

## Expand description

Crate `retry` provides utilities for retrying operations that can fail.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Retry an operation using the [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) function.

[accepts an iterator over](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry`[s and a closure that returns a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`Duration`[(or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[; see below). The iterator is used to determine how long to wait after each unsuccessful try and how many times to try before giving up and returning](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult`[. The closure determines either the final successful value, or an error value, which can either be returned immediately or used to indicate that the operation should be retried.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Result::Err`Any type that implements [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with an associated

`Item` type of [can be used to determine retry behavior, though a few useful implementations are provided in the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`Duration`[module, including a fixed delay and exponential backoff.](https://docs.rs/delay/index.html)

`delay````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_ok());
```
The [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) API can be used to limit or modify the delay strategy. For example, to limit
the number of retries to 1:

```
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100).take(1), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_err());
```
To apply random jitter to any delay strategy, the [ delay::jitter](https://docs.rs/delay/fn.jitter.html) function can be used in
combination with the

[API:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Exponential::from_millis(10).map(jitter).take(3), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_ok());
```
To deal with fatal errors, return [ OperationResult](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html), which is like

[, but with a third case to distinguish between errors that should cause a retry and errors that should immediately return, halting retry behavior. (Internally,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[is always used, and closures passed to](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult`[that return plain](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry`[are converted into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[.)](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult````
use retry::OperationResult;
let mut collection = vec![1, 2].into_iter();
let value = retry(Fixed::from_millis(1), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 2 => OperationResult::Ok(n),
        Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("not 2"),
        None => OperationResult::Err("not found"),
    }
}).unwrap();
assert_eq!(value, 2);
```
If your operation needs to know how many times it’s been tried, use the [ retry_with_index](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_with_index.html)
function. This works the same as

[, but passes the number of the current try to the closure as an argument.](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5].into_iter();
let result = retry_with_index(Fixed::from_millis(100), |current_try| {
    if current_try > 3 {
        return OperationResult::Err("did not succeed within 3 tries");
    }
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 5 => OperationResult::Ok("n is 5!"),
        Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("n must be 5!"),
        None => OperationResult::Retry("n was never 5!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_err());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `random`: offer some random delay utilities (on by default)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [delay](https://docs.rs/delay/index.html)
- Different types of delay for retryable operations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error with a retryable operation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Operation](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)- Result
- A result that represents either success, retryable failure, or immediately-returning failure.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)
- Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given `Duration`
- [retry_](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_with_index.html)- with_ - index
- Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given `Duration`

[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! Retry an operation using the [`retry`] function. [`retry`] accepts an iterator over
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! [`Duration`]s and a closure that returns a [`Result`] (or [`OperationResult`]; see below). The
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! iterator is used to determine how long to wait after each unsuccessful try and how many times to
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! try before giving up and returning [`Result::Err`]. The closure determines either the final
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! successful value, or an error value, which can either be returned immediately or used to
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! indicate that the operation should be retried.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! Any type that implements [`Iterator`] with an associated `Item` type of [`Duration`] can be
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! used to determine retry behavior, though a few useful implementations are provided in the
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! [`delay`] module, including a fixed delay and exponential backoff.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! ```
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! # use retry::retry;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! # use retry::delay::Fixed;
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100), || {
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     match collection.next() {
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!         Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!         Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!         None => Err("n was never 3!"),
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!     }
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! });
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! assert!(result.is_ok());
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! ```
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! The [`Iterator`] API can be used to limit or modify the delay strategy. For example, to limit
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! the number of retries to 1:
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! # use retry::retry;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! # use retry::delay::Fixed;
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100).take(1), || {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     match collection.next() {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!         Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!         Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!         None => Err("n was never 3!"),
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!     }
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! });
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! assert!(result.is_err());
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ```
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)#![cfg_attr(
[52](https://docs.rs#52)    feature = "random",
[53](https://docs.rs#53)    doc = r##"
[54](https://docs.rs#54)To apply random jitter to any delay strategy, the [`delay::jitter`] function can be used in
[55](https://docs.rs#55)combination with the [`Iterator`] API:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)```
[58](https://docs.rs#58)# use retry::retry;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)# use retry::delay::{Exponential, jitter};
[60](https://docs.rs#60)let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
[61](https://docs.rs#61)
[62](https://docs.rs#62)let result = retry(Exponential::from_millis(10).map(jitter).take(3), || {
[63](https://docs.rs#63)    match collection.next() {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
[65](https://docs.rs#65)        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
[66](https://docs.rs#66)        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    }
[68](https://docs.rs#68)});
[69](https://docs.rs#69)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)assert!(result.is_ok());
[71](https://docs.rs#71)```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)"##
[73](https://docs.rs#73))]
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! To deal with fatal errors, return [`OperationResult`], which is like [`Result`], but with a
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! third case to distinguish between errors that should cause a retry and errors that should
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! immediately return, halting retry behavior. (Internally, [`OperationResult`] is always used, and
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! closures passed to [`retry`] that return plain [`Result`] are converted into
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! [`OperationResult`].)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! ```
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! # use retry::retry;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! # use retry::delay::Fixed;
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! use retry::OperationResult;
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! let mut collection = vec![1, 2].into_iter();
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! let value = retry(Fixed::from_millis(1), || {
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     match collection.next() {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!         Some(n) if n == 2 => OperationResult::Ok(n),
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!         Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("not 2"),
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!         None => OperationResult::Err("not found"),
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     }
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! }).unwrap();
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! assert_eq!(value, 2);
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! ```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! If your operation needs to know how many times it's been tried, use the [`retry_with_index`]
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! function. This works the same as [`retry`], but passes the number of the current try to the
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! closure as an argument.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ```
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! # use retry::retry_with_index;
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! # use retry::delay::Fixed;
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! # use retry::OperationResult;
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5].into_iter();
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! let result = retry_with_index(Fixed::from_millis(100), |current_try| {
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!     if current_try > 3 {
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!         return OperationResult::Err("did not succeed within 3 tries");
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!     }
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!     match collection.next() {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!         Some(n) if n == 5 => OperationResult::Ok("n is 5!"),
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!         Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("n must be 5!"),
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!         None => OperationResult::Retry("n was never 5!"),
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!     }
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! });
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! assert!(result.is_err());
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! ```
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!

[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// iterator ends.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)pub fn retry<I, O, R, E, OR>(iterable: I, mut operation: O) -> Result<R, Error<E>>
[144](https://docs.rs#144)where
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    I: IntoIterator<Item = Duration>,
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    O: FnMut() -> OR,

[150](https://docs.rs#150)}
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given [`Duration`]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// iterator ends, with each iteration of the operation receiving the number of the attempt as an
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// argument.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)pub fn retry_with_index<I, O, R, E, OR>(iterable: I, mut operation: O) -> Result<R, Error<E>>
[156](https://docs.rs#156)where
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    I: IntoIterator<Item = Duration>,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    O: FnMut(u64) -> OR,
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    OR: Into<OperationResult<R, E>>,
[160](https://docs.rs#160){
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    let mut iterator = iterable.into_iter();
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    let mut current_try = 1;
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    let mut total_delay = Duration::default();
[164](https://docs.rs#164)
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    loop {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        match operation(current_try).into() {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            OperationResult::Ok(value) => return Ok(value),
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            OperationResult::Retry(error) => {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)                if let Some(delay) = iterator.next() {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)                    sleep(delay);
[171](https://docs.rs#171)                    current_try += 1;
[172](https://docs.rs#172)                    total_delay += delay;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)                } else {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)                    return Err(Error {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)                        error,
[176](https://docs.rs#176)                        total_delay,
[177](https://docs.rs#177)                        tries: current_try,
[178](https://docs.rs#178)                    });
[179](https://docs.rs#179)                }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            }
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            OperationResult::Err(error) => {
[182](https://docs.rs#182)                return Err(Error {
[183](https://docs.rs#183)                    error,
[184](https://docs.rs#184)                    total_delay,
[185](https://docs.rs#185)                    tries: current_try,
[186](https://docs.rs#186)                });
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)}

# OperationResult in retry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/retry/2.2.0/retry/enum.OperationResult.html

```
pub enum OperationResult<T, E> {
    Ok(T),
    Retry(E),
    Err(E),
}
```
## Expand description

A result that represents either success, retryable failure, or immediately-returning failure.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Ok)

### Ok(T)

Contains the success value.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Retry)

### Retry(E)

Contains the error value if duration is exceeded.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Err)

### Err(E)

Contains an error value to return immediately.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/retry/opresult.rs.html#42-111)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-OperationResult%3CT,+E%3E)### impl<T, E> [OperationResult](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/retry/opresult.rs.html#42-111)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-OperationResult%3CT,+E%3E)

### impl<T, E> [OperationResult](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)<T, E>

Returns `true` if the result is [ OperationResult::Ok](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html#variant.Ok).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Ok(-3);
assert_eq!(x.is_ok(), true);
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Retry("Some error message");
assert_eq!(x.is_ok(), false);
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Err("Some other error message");
assert_eq!(x.is_ok(), false);
```
Returns `true` if the result is [ OperationResult::Retry](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html#variant.Retry).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Ok(-3);
assert_eq!(x.is_retry(), false);
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Retry("Some error message");
assert_eq!(x.is_retry(), true);
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Err("Some other error message");
assert_eq!(x.is_retry(), false);
```
Returns `true` if the result is [ OperationResult::Err](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html#variant.Err).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Ok(-3);
assert_eq!(x.is_err(), false);
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Retry("Some error message");
assert_eq!(x.is_err(), false);
let x: OperationResult<i32, &str> = OperationResult::Err("Some other error message");
assert_eq!(x.is_err(), true);
```

# retry::delay - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/retry/2.2.0/retry/delay/index.html

## Expand description

Different types of delay for retryable operations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Exponential](https://docs.rs/struct.Exponential.html)
- Each retry increases the delay since the last exponentially.
- [Fibonacci](https://docs.rs/struct.Fibonacci.html)
- Each retry uses a delay which is the sum of the two previous delays.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.Fixed.html)
- Each retry uses a fixed delay.
- [NoDelay](https://docs.rs/struct.NoDelay.html)
- Each retry happens immediately without any delay.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/struct.Range.html)
- Each retry uses a duration randomly chosen from a range. (When the `random`Cargo feature is enabled.)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [jitter](https://docs.rs/fn.jitter.html)
- Apply full random jitter to a duration. (When the `random`Cargo feature is enabled.)

# retry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/retry/latest/retry/

## Expand description

Crate `retry` provides utilities for retrying operations that can fail.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Retry an operation using the [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) function.

[accepts an iterator over](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry`[s and a closure that returns a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`Duration`[(or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[; see below). The iterator is used to determine how long to wait after each unsuccessful try and how many times to try before giving up and returning](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult`[. The closure determines either the final successful value, or an error value, which can either be returned immediately or used to indicate that the operation should be retried.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Result::Err`Any type that implements [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with an associated

`Item` type of [can be used to determine retry behavior, though a few useful implementations are provided in the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`Duration`[module, including a fixed delay and exponential backoff.](https://docs.rs/delay/index.html)

`delay````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_ok());
```
The [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) API can be used to limit or modify the delay strategy. For example, to limit
the number of retries to 1:

```
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100).take(1), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_err());
```
To apply random jitter to any delay strategy, the [ delay::jitter](https://docs.rs/delay/fn.jitter.html) function can be used in
combination with the

[API:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Exponential::from_millis(10).map(jitter).take(3), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_ok());
```
To deal with fatal errors, return [ OperationResult](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html), which is like

[, but with a third case to distinguish between errors that should cause a retry and errors that should immediately return, halting retry behavior. (Internally,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[is always used, and closures passed to](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult`[that return plain](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry`[are converted into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[.)](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult````
use retry::OperationResult;
let mut collection = vec![1, 2].into_iter();
let value = retry(Fixed::from_millis(1), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 2 => OperationResult::Ok(n),
        Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("not 2"),
        None => OperationResult::Err("not found"),
    }
}).unwrap();
assert_eq!(value, 2);
```
If your operation needs to know how many times it’s been tried, use the [ retry_with_index](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_with_index.html)
function. This works the same as

[, but passes the number of the current try to the closure as an argument.](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5].into_iter();
let result = retry_with_index(Fixed::from_millis(100), |current_try| {
    if current_try > 3 {
        return OperationResult::Err("did not succeed within 3 tries");
    }
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 5 => OperationResult::Ok("n is 5!"),
        Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("n must be 5!"),
        None => OperationResult::Retry("n was never 5!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_err());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `random`: offer some random delay utilities (on by default)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [delay](https://docs.rs/delay/index.html)
- Different types of delay for retryable operations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error with a retryable operation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Operation](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)- Result
- A result that represents either success, retryable failure, or immediately-returning failure.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)
- Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given `Duration`
- [retry_](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_with_index.html)- with_ - index
- Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given `Duration`

# rand 0.9.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/^0.9

# Rand

Rand is a set of crates supporting (pseudo-)random generators:

- Built over a standard RNG trait: `rand_core::RngCore`
- With fast implementations of both [strong](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[small](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators:`rand::rngs``rand_chacha``rand_xoshiro``rand_pcg`[rngs repo](https://github.com/rust-random/rngs/)
- `rand::rng`- `std`targets
- Direct support for seeding generators from the [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate

With broad support for random value generation and random processes:

- `StandardUniform`- `Uniform`- [more](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/distr/index.html)
- Samplers for a large number of non-uniform random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- Random processes (mostly choose and shuffle) via `rand::seq`

All with:

- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations thanks to contributions from the wide user-base

Rand **is not**:

- Small (LoC). Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Primarily a cryptographic library. `rand`does provide some generators which aim to support unpredictable value generation under certain constraints; see[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/SECURITY.md)for details. Users are expected to determine for themselves whether`rand`'s functionality meets their own security requirements.

Documentation:

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. Current `MAJOR.MINOR` versions are:

- Version 0.9 was released in January 2025.

See the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) or [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html) for more details.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator
- `os_rng`(implied by- `std`) enables- `rngs::OsRng`, using the- [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate
- `std_rng`enables inclusion of- `StdRng`,- `ThreadRng`
- `small_rng`enables inclusion of the- `SmallRng`PRNG

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

-
`nightly`includes some additions requiring nightly Rust
-
`simd_support`(experimental) enables sampling of SIMD values (uniformly random SIMD integers and floats), requiring nightly Rust
-
`unbiased`use unbiased sampling for algorithms supporting this option: Uniform distribution.(By default, bias affecting no more than one in 2^48 samples is accepted.) Note: enabling this option is expected to affect reproducibility of results.

Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and
compiler versions will be compatible. This is especially true of Rand's
experimental `simd_support` feature.

Rand supports limited functionality in `no_std` mode (enabled via
`default-features = false`). In this case, `OsRng` and `from_os_rng` are
unavailable (unless `os_rng` is enabled), large parts of `seq` are
unavailable (unless `alloc` is enabled), and `ThreadRng` is unavailable.

## Portability and platform support

Many (but not all) algorithms are intended to have reproducible output. Read more in the book: [Portability](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html).

The Rand library supports a variety of CPU architectures. Platform integration is outsourced to [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom).

### WebAssembly support

The [WASI](https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI/tree/main) and Emscripten
targets are directly supported. The `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target is not
*automatically* supported. To enable support for this target, refer to the
[ getrandom documentation for WebAssembly](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).
Alternatively, the

`os_rng` feature may be disabled.# License

Rand is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# retry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/retry

## Expand description

Crate `retry` provides utilities for retrying operations that can fail.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Retry an operation using the [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) function.

[accepts an iterator over](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry`[s and a closure that returns a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`Duration`[(or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[; see below). The iterator is used to determine how long to wait after each unsuccessful try and how many times to try before giving up and returning](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult`[. The closure determines either the final successful value, or an error value, which can either be returned immediately or used to indicate that the operation should be retried.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Result::Err`Any type that implements [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with an associated

`Item` type of [can be used to determine retry behavior, though a few useful implementations are provided in the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`Duration`[module, including a fixed delay and exponential backoff.](https://docs.rs/delay/index.html)

`delay````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_ok());
```
The [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) API can be used to limit or modify the delay strategy. For example, to limit
the number of retries to 1:

```
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Fixed::from_millis(100).take(1), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_err());
```
To apply random jitter to any delay strategy, the [ delay::jitter](https://docs.rs/delay/fn.jitter.html) function can be used in
combination with the

[API:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3].into_iter();
let result = retry(Exponential::from_millis(10).map(jitter).take(3), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 3 => Ok("n is 3!"),
        Some(_) => Err("n must be 3!"),
        None => Err("n was never 3!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_ok());
```
To deal with fatal errors, return [ OperationResult](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html), which is like

[, but with a third case to distinguish between errors that should cause a retry and errors that should immediately return, halting retry behavior. (Internally,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[is always used, and closures passed to](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult`[that return plain](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry`[are converted into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[.)](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)

`OperationResult````
use retry::OperationResult;
let mut collection = vec![1, 2].into_iter();
let value = retry(Fixed::from_millis(1), || {
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 2 => OperationResult::Ok(n),
        Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("not 2"),
        None => OperationResult::Err("not found"),
    }
}).unwrap();
assert_eq!(value, 2);
```
If your operation needs to know how many times it’s been tried, use the [ retry_with_index](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_with_index.html)
function. This works the same as

[, but passes the number of the current try to the closure as an argument.](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)

`retry````
let mut collection = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5].into_iter();
let result = retry_with_index(Fixed::from_millis(100), |current_try| {
    if current_try > 3 {
        return OperationResult::Err("did not succeed within 3 tries");
    }
    match collection.next() {
        Some(n) if n == 5 => OperationResult::Ok("n is 5!"),
        Some(_) => OperationResult::Retry("n must be 5!"),
        None => OperationResult::Retry("n was never 5!"),
    }
});
assert!(result.is_err());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `random`: offer some random delay utilities (on by default)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [delay](https://docs.rs/delay/index.html)
- Different types of delay for retryable operations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error with a retryable operation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Operation](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationResult.html)- Result
- A result that represents either success, retryable failure, or immediately-returning failure.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html)
- Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given `Duration`
- [retry_](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_with_index.html)- with_ - index
- Retry the given operation synchronously until it succeeds, or until the given `Duration`

# rand 0.9.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/0.9.4

# Rand

Rand is a set of crates supporting (pseudo-)random generators:

- Built over a standard RNG trait: `rand_core::RngCore`
- With fast implementations of both [strong](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[small](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators:`rand::rngs``rand_chacha``rand_xoshiro``rand_pcg`[rngs repo](https://github.com/rust-random/rngs/)
- `rand::rng`- `std`targets
- Direct support for seeding generators from the [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate

With broad support for random value generation and random processes:

- `StandardUniform`- `Uniform`- [more](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/distr/index.html)
- Samplers for a large number of non-uniform random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- Random processes (mostly choose and shuffle) via `rand::seq`

All with:

- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations thanks to contributions from the wide user-base

Rand **is not**:

- Small (LoC). Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Primarily a cryptographic library. `rand`does provide some generators which aim to support unpredictable value generation under certain constraints; see[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/SECURITY.md)for details. Users are expected to determine for themselves whether`rand`'s functionality meets their own security requirements.

Documentation:

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. Current `MAJOR.MINOR` versions are:

- Version 0.9 was released in January 2025.

See the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) or [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html) for more details.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator
- `os_rng`(implied by- `std`) enables- `rngs::OsRng`, using the- [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate
- `std_rng`enables inclusion of- `StdRng`,- `ThreadRng`
- `small_rng`enables inclusion of the- `SmallRng`PRNG

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

-
`nightly`includes some additions requiring nightly Rust
-
`simd_support`(experimental) enables sampling of SIMD values (uniformly random SIMD integers and floats), requiring nightly Rust
-
`unbiased`use unbiased sampling for algorithms supporting this option: Uniform distribution.(By default, bias affecting no more than one in 2^48 samples is accepted.) Note: enabling this option is expected to affect reproducibility of results.

Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and
compiler versions will be compatible. This is especially true of Rand's
experimental `simd_support` feature.

Rand supports limited functionality in `no_std` mode (enabled via
`default-features = false`). In this case, `OsRng` and `from_os_rng` are
unavailable (unless `os_rng` is enabled), large parts of `seq` are
unavailable (unless `alloc` is enabled), and `ThreadRng` is unavailable.

## Portability and platform support

Many (but not all) algorithms are intended to have reproducible output. Read more in the book: [Portability](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html).

The Rand library supports a variety of CPU architectures. Platform integration is outsourced to [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom).

### WebAssembly support

The [WASI](https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI/tree/main) and Emscripten
targets are directly supported. The `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target is not
*automatically* supported. To enable support for this target, refer to the
[ getrandom documentation for WebAssembly](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).
Alternatively, the

`os_rng` feature may be disabled.# License

Rand is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# rand_chacha - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_chacha/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

The ChaCha random number generators.

These are native Rust implementations of RNGs derived from the
[ChaCha stream ciphers](https://cr.yp.to/chacha.html) by D J Bernstein.

[§](https://docs.rs#generators)Generators

This crate provides 8-, 12- and 20-round variants of generators via a “core”
implementation (of [ BlockRngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/trait.BlockRngCore.html)), each with an associated “RNG” type
(implementing

[).](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html)

`RngCore`These generators are all deterministic and portable (see [Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html)
in the book), with testing against reference vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#cryptographic-secure-usage)Cryptographic (secure) usage

Where secure unpredictable generators are required, it is suggested to use
[ ChaCha12Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Rng.html) or

[and to seed via](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Rng.html)

`ChaCha20Rng`[.](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html#method.from_os_rng)

`SeedableRng::from_os_rng`See also the [Security](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#security) chapter in the rand book. The crate is provided
“as is”, without any form of guarantee, and without a security audit.

[§](https://docs.rs#seeding-construction)Seeding (construction)

Generators implement the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait. Any method may be used,
but note that

`seed_from_u64` is not suitable for usage where security is
important. Some suggestions:- With a fresh seed, **direct from the OS**(implies a syscall):`let rng = ChaCha12Rng::from_os_rng();`
- **From a master generator.**This could be- `rand::rng`- `ChaCha20Rng`

See also [Seeding RNGs](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-seeding.html) in the book.

[§](https://docs.rs#generation)Generation

Generators implement [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html), whose methods may be used directly to
generate unbounded integer or byte values.

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, RngCore};
use rand_chacha::ChaCha12Rng;
let mut rng = ChaCha12Rng::from_seed(Default::default());
let x = rng.next_u64();
assert_eq!(x, 0x53f955076a9af49b);
```
It is often more convenient to use the [ rand::Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.rng.html) trait, which provides
further functionality. See also the

[Random Values](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-values.html)chapter in the book.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ChaCha8](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha8Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 8 rounds
- [ChaCha8](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha8Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.
- [ChaCha12](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 12 rounds
- [ChaCha12](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.
- [ChaCha20](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 20 rounds
- [ChaCha20](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [ChaCha](https://docs.rs/type.ChaChaCore.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 20 rounds, low-level interface
- [ChaCha](https://docs.rs/type.ChaChaRng.html)- Rng
- ChaCha with 20 rounds

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

Random number generation traits

This crate is mainly of interest to crates publishing implementations of
[ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html). Other users are encouraged to use the

[crate instead which re-exports the main traits and error types.](https://docs.rs/rand)

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.103/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1.2.1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of [PCG generators](https://www.pcg-random.org/).
The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in
other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

[§](https://docs.rs#generators)Generators

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`- `Lcg64Xsh32`- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`- `Lcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`- `Mcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

These generators are all deterministic and portable (see [Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html)
in the book), with testing against reference vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#seeding-construction)Seeding (construction)

Generators implement the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait. All methods are suitable for
seeding. Some suggestions:

- To automatically seed with a unique seed, use `SeedableRng::from_rng``rand::rng()`
- Seed **from an integer**via`seed_from_u64`. This uses a hash function internally to yield a (typically) good seed from any input.`let rng = Pcg64Mcg::seed_from_u64(1);`

See also [Seeding RNGs](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-seeding.html) in the book.

[§](https://docs.rs#generation)Generation

Generators implement [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html), whose methods may be used directly to
generate unbounded integer or byte values.

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, RngCore};
use rand_pcg::Pcg64Mcg;
let mut rng = Pcg64Mcg::seed_from_u64(0);
let x = rng.next_u64();
assert_eq!(x, 0x5603f242407deca2);
```
It is often more convenient to use the [ rand::Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.rng.html) trait, which provides
further functionality. See also the

[Random Values](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-values.html)chapter in the book.

# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1.7/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [broadcast](https://docs.rs/fn.broadcast.html)
- Executes `op`within every thread in the current thread pool. If this is called from a non-Rayon thread, it will execute in the global thread pool. Any attempts to use`join`,`scope`, or parallel iterators will then operate within that thread pool. When the call has completed on each thread, returns a vector containing all of their return values.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the number of threads in the current registry. If this code is executing within a Rayon thread pool, then this will be the number of threads for the thread pool of the current thread. Otherwise, it will be the number of threads for the global thread pool.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_thread_index.html)- thread_ - index
- If called from a Rayon worker thread, returns the index of that
thread within its current pool; if not called from a Rayon thread,
returns `None`.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope.html)- place_ - scope
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope_fifo.html)- place_ - scope_ - fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [join](https://docs.rs/fn.join.html)
- Takes two closures and *potentially*runs them in parallel. It returns a pair of the results from those closures.
- [join_](https://docs.rs/fn.join_context.html)- context
- Identical to `join`, except that the closures have a parameter that provides context for the way the closure has been called, especially indicating whether they’re executing on a different thread than where`join_context`was called. This will occur if the second job is stolen by a different thread, or if`join_context`was called from outside the thread pool to begin with.
- [max_](https://docs.rs/fn.max_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the maximum number of threads that Rayon supports in a single thread pool.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [scope_](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)- fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Puts the task into the Rayon thread pool’s job queue in the “static”
or “global” scope. Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)to create a scope.`scope()`function
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_broadcast.html)- broadcast
- Spawns an asynchronous task on every thread in this thread pool. This task
will run in the implicit, global scope, which means that it may outlast the
current stack frame – therefore, it cannot capture any references onto the
stack (you will likely need a `move`closure).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_fifo.html)- fifo
- Fires off a task into the Rayon thread pool in the “static” or
“global” scope.  Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)to create a scope.`scope_fifo()`function
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_local.html)- local
- Cooperatively yields execution to local Rayon work.
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_now.html)- now
- Cooperatively yields execution to Rayon.
